The [**normal distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is a symmetric location-scale family. Its parameters should be estimated from the linguistic measurement at hand, and its shape should be compared with those observations rather than assumed from the name of the variable.

Why use it as a reference for F1? A continuous measurement perturbed by many
small additive sources may be approximately symmetric within a sufficiently
homogeneous speaker group. That argument assumes [independent observations](../foundations/independence.qmd),
one stable location and scale within group, and tails adequately represented
by a symmetric bell shape. F1 is positive while the normal support is all real
numbers, so the approximation is defensible only when negligible fitted mass
falls below zero and the deviations from each fitted group mean have a shape
compatible with the model.

We define the location–scale density, estimate it separately by speaker group, and then check its support and shape assumptions against the observed /i/ F1 values.

## Definition

For $X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

The parameters are the [expected value](expected-values.qmd) and
[variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd):

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\sigma^2.
$$

Because the centered distance is squared,

$$
f_X(\mu-d)=f_X(\mu+d).
$$

Thus $\mu$ controls location while $\sigma$ controls scale. Standardization gives

$$
Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X\leq x)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right),
$$

where

$$
\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-t^2/2}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

## Fitting /i/ F1 by speaker group

We return to the [Hillenbrand et al. vowel data introduced earlier](continuous-random-variables.qmd). Each speaker produced one /hVd/ token for each vowel, so restricting to /i/ leaves one F1 measurement per speaker. The complete acoustic table supports this comparison because the F1 source column has no missing values.

The /i/ restriction avoids mixing vowel categories, and separate speaker-group
fits avoid forcing boys, girls, men, and women to share one acoustic location
and scale. These choices describe observed design strata; they do not make the
groups population samples.

```{r}
#| label: fit-hillenbrand-normal
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
i_tokens <- subset(vowels, vowel == "i")

fits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(i_tokens, i_tokens$speaker_type), function(z) {
  mu <- mean(z$f1_hz)
  sigma <- sqrt(mean((z$f1_hz - mu)^2))
  data.frame(speaker_type = z$speaker_type[1], n = nrow(z),
             mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
}))
row.names(fits) <- NULL

normal_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(i_tokens, i_tokens$speaker_type), function(z) {
  mu <- mean(z$f1_hz)
  sigma <- sqrt(mean((z$f1_hz - mu)^2))
  values <- seq(min(z$f1_hz) - 20, max(z$f1_hz) + 20, length.out = 300L)
  data.frame(speaker_type = z$speaker_type[1], f1_hz = values,
             density = dnorm(values, mu, sigma))
}))

stopifnot(
  nrow(vowels) == 1668L,
  nrow(i_tokens) == 139L,
  !anyDuplicated(i_tokens$speaker_id),
  all(is.finite(fits$mu)), all(fits$sigma > 0)
)

fits
```

**Maximum likelihood** chooses the parameter values that maximize the joint
density of the observed sample under the stated independent normal model. The
later [maximum-likelihood
page](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) develops the principle
in general. For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, it gives

$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\widehat\mu)^2.
$$

Taking the [natural
logarithm](../foundations/zipfs-law.qmd#likelihoods-and-logarithms) turns the
independent density product into a sum. Up to an additive constant, the normal
log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)
=-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2.
$$

The [derivative is a local rate of
change](expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change). Holding
$\sigma^2$ fixed and setting the log-likelihood slope with respect to $\mu$ to
zero gives
$\sum_i(x_i-\widehat\mu)=0$, hence $\widehat\mu=\bar x$. Substituting that
value and setting the local slope with respect to $\sigma^2$ to zero gives the
$1/n$ mean squared deviation above. The $1/(n-1)$ sample variance is a separate
unbiased estimator, not the normal MLE. In the code, the split F1 rows supply
the realized $x_i$, `mu` is $\widehat\mu$, and `sigma^2` is
$\widehat\sigma^2$.

The observed group rows determine the fitted locations and spreads; neither is
selected in advance.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-normal
#| fig-cap: "Observed /i/ F1 measurements and group-specific fitted normal densities. Each facet contains one token per speaker."
ggplot(i_tokens, aes(f1_hz)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 9,
                 fill = "grey78", color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = normal_grid, aes(f1_hz, density),
            color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker_type, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "/i/ F1 (Hz)", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

A histogram overlay can hide tail and quantile discrepancies. A
[residual](../regression-models/residuals.qmd) is an observed value minus its
fitted location. The following normal-quantile diagnostic standardizes these
within group and compares their ordered values with standard-normal quantiles.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-normal-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal-quantile diagnostics for group-standardized /i/ F1 measurements. Systematic curvature would indicate a mismatch in distribution shape."
i_tokens$standardized_residual <- ave(
  i_tokens$f1_hz,
  i_tokens$speaker_type,
  FUN = function(x) {
    sigma_mle <- sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))
    (x - mean(x)) / sigma_mle
  }
)

ggplot(i_tokens, aes(sample = standardized_residual)) +
  stat_qq(color = "grey45") +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#8B1A1A") +
  facet_wrap(~speaker_type, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Standard-normal quantile", y = "Standardized observed quantile") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The overlays provide a descriptive reference. They do not establish normal sampling, and the source design supports claims about these recorded /hVd/ productions rather than spontaneous speech.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify one row of `fits` directly from the raw measurements.
2. Why does the MLE for $\sigma^2$ divide by $n$ rather than $n-1$?
3. Standardize the adult-men measurements with their fitted parameters and inspect the resulting histogram.
4. Which source restriction makes the within-facet observations nonrepeated by speaker?
5. What pattern in the quantile plot would challenge the normal reference even
   if the histogram overlay looked adequate?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. For adult men, the 45 raw /i/ F1 measurements have mean 342.688889 Hz and population-standard-deviation estimate 27.915596 Hz, matching the `fits` row. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The normal MLE divides by $n$ because maximizing the likelihood estimates mean squared deviation directly; division by $n-1$ is a separate unbiasedness correction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Standardizing adult-men values as $(F1-342.688889)/27.915596$ produces values with empirical mean zero and population standard deviation one while retaining the histogram's observed shape. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Restricting each facet to one vowel category leaves one measurement per speaker, so no speaker is repeated within a facet. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Systematic curvature or extreme points far from the reference line would
   indicate tail or shape discrepancies hidden by histogram binning.

</details>

The normal family provides a symmetric additive-error reference on the real
line. Its MLE variance uses $n$, not the unbiased $n-1$ denominator, and
residual quantiles assess the fitted shape beyond what a histogram overlay can
show. The [chi-squared distribution](chi-squared-distribution.qmd) next
describes a variance statistic under stronger normal-sampling assumptions.
